learningObjectives: Explain the relationship between a Process in the Case Life Cycle and a Process diagram in the Process Modeler
Identify Process diagram shapes by color and purpose, and distinguish Connector Actions from Local Actions

elements.description: A series of Steps expected to occur in a logical, sequential order. When you add a Process to a Case Type in the Case Life Cycle designer, the Steps are configured in the typical sequence to completion.

elements.text: Decision shapes in a process flow are like railroad switches: when a train (case) arrives at a switch point, the switch (decision) checks the rail conditions (data values) and automatically routes the train down track A or track B — no driver needed, no delay. The correct track is always taken as long as the conditions are correctly configured.

elements.description: Pega's visual canvas for advanced flow control. Shapes include Assignments, Automations, Decisions, and Subprocesses. Use the Process diagram when the Case Life Cycle's stage/step view doesn't support the required branching or parallel logic.

Click the CONFIGURE PROCESS icon located on the Process in the Case Life Cycle. This opens the PROCESS MODELER, where you add, edit, and remove shapes in the Process diagram to build configurations that deviate from the logical sequential order.

elements.caption: Every Process diagram includes a Start (green circle) and End (red circle) by default. Collect information / Assignment = green rectangle; Subprocess = blue rectangle; Automation = yellow rectangle; Decision = orange diamond. Connectors are the arrows linking shapes.

elements.description: Orange diamond that adds conditional branching or skipping to a Process. Advances the Case automatically based on one or more conditions — no user action required at this shape. Supports more than one outcome path.
Decision automation frees operators to focus on complex cases:
items: AUTOMATE — straightforward decisions with clear rules (e.g., credit score below threshold → auto-deny)
HUMAN expertise — ambiguous cases needing judgment (e.g., low credit score but high salary and strong history → agent review)

elements.description: (1) Cases move forward but may include ANOTHER STEP as needed — you choose when extra processing supports the Case. (2) Cases go to ANOTHER STAGE using the Change Stage shape; by skipping a Stage you support out-of-sequence processing.

elements.description: Defines what a user can do at a specific Assignment Step — which form appears, which fields are shown, and what submit options are available. Controls user interaction within a Step, not the path between Steps.
Within a Process, you associate a Flow Action with a CONNECTOR (the arrow between shapes) or an ASSIGNMENT shape (a green rectangle in the Process diagram).
Completes the Assignment AND advances the Case to the next shape. A Connector Action is configured as a LINE shape (the connector) in the Process Modeler.
Updates the Assignment but does NOT advance the Case to the next shape. A Local Action is configured in the PROPERTIES PANE of an Assignment shape in the Process Modeler.

examPitfalls.title: Process vs Process diagram
examPitfalls.trapDescription: A Process is a series of Steps in logical sequential order; the Process diagram is the advanced view used when the path is NOT sequential.
examPitfalls.bestPractice: Use the Process diagram (Process Modeler) when Steps must branch or skip the typical order.

examPitfalls.title: Opening the Process Modeler
examPitfalls.trapDescription: You access the Process diagram from the Configure Process icon on the Process — not from a separate menu or App Studio settings.
examPitfalls.bestPractice: Click the Configure Process icon on the Process in the Case Life Cycle to open the Process Modeler.

examPitfalls.title: Shape colors get swapped
examPitfalls.trapDescription: Exam swaps shape colors: Decision = orange diamond, Automation = yellow rectangle, Subprocess = blue rectangle, Collect information / Assignment = green rectangle.
examPitfalls.bestPractice: Memorize: orange diamond = Decision; yellow = Automation; blue = Subprocess; green = Collect/Assignment; Start = green circle, End = red circle.

examPitfalls.title: Decision shapes advance automatically
examPitfalls.trapDescription: A Decision shape advances the Process automatically based on business logic or Conditions — it is not a user picking a path.
examPitfalls.bestPractice: Use a Decision shape to add a conditional path that supports more than one outcome without human input.

examPitfalls.title: Connector vs Local Action behavior
examPitfalls.trapDescription: Questions describe a flow that uses a Connector and ask what happens when it fires. Candidates say it sends the case to a subprocess and continues the main flow after. A Connector transfers control to the target — the original flow does not resume. A Local Action, by contrast, executes a subprocess and then returns to the calling step.
examPitfalls.bestPractice: Need to move to the next shape → Connector Action. Need to update in place → Local Action.

examPitfalls.title: Where each Flow Action is configured
examPitfalls.trapDescription: Connector Action = configured as a line shape (the connector); Local Action = configured in the properties pane of an Assignment shape.
examPitfalls.bestPractice: Connector → the line between shapes; Local → the Assignment shape's properties pane.

examPitfalls.title: Skipping a Stage = Change Stage shape
examPitfalls.trapDescription: Out-of-sequence processing is achieved by a Decision flow that uses the Change Stage shape to move the Case to a different Stage.
examPitfalls.bestPractice: Use the Change Stage shape to skip a Stage and support out-of-sequence processing.

practiceQuiz.scenario: A Business Architect new to Pega is learning about Case Life Cycle design and asks an SA to explain what a Process represents within a Case Life Cycle, and how it relates to the Steps inside it. How does Pega Platform define a Process within a Case Life Cycle?

options.text: A series of Steps expected to occur in a logical, sequential order
A reusable Decision Table that returns one of several outcomes
A single user form displayed during an Assignment
A graphical diagram that always processes Steps out of sequence

practiceQuiz.hint: Recall the official Pega definition of a Process — what order do Steps follow within it?
practiceQuiz.rationale: A Process is a series of Steps expected to occur in a logical, sequential order. B is a decision rule, not a Process. C is a Flow Action/form, not a Process. D is wrong — sequential order is the default; the Process diagram is what enables non-sequential paths.

practiceQuiz.scenario: An SA is explaining to a new developer why Pega introduced the Process diagram in addition to the standard Case Life Cycle Stage structure. The developer wants to understand the problem the Process diagram was designed to solve. Why did Pega Platform introduce the Process diagram as part of Case design?

options.text: Because business processes do not often follow a sequential path, the Process diagram allows advanced configurations that control the path to resolution
To replace the Case Life Cycle designer entirely with a diagram-only authoring model
To store reusable Decision Tables and Decision Trees in one place
To let users manually choose every path the Case takes at run time

practiceQuiz.hint: Think about why the Process diagram was introduced — what limitation of sequential flow does it address?
practiceQuiz.rationale: Because business processes often deviate from a sequential path, the Process diagram provides advanced configurations that control the path toward resolution. B is wrong — the Case Life Cycle and Process diagram work together. C describes decision rules, not the Process diagram. D is wrong — the diagram automates the path, it doesn't force manual selection.

practiceQuiz.scenario: How do you open the Process diagram to add, edit, and remove shapes?

options.text: Click the Configure Process icon on the Process in the Case Life Cycle, which opens the Process Modeler
Open the Records Explorer and edit the Flow rule XML directly
Switch to App Studio Settings and enable diagram mode
Click the Start shape in the Case summary panel at run time

practiceQuiz.hint: Click the Configure Process icon on a Step to open the Process Modeler.
practiceQuiz.rationale: You access the Process diagram by clicking the Configure Process icon on the Process in the Case Life Cycle, which opens the Process Modeler. B, C, and D are not how the Process Modeler is opened.

practiceQuiz.scenario: A new Pega developer opens the Process Modeler for the first time after creating a new Process and wants to understand what shapes are present by default before any Steps are added. Which two shapes does every newly created Pega Process diagram include by default?

options.text: A Start shape (green circle) and an End shape (red circle)
A Decision shape (orange diamond) and an Automation shape (yellow rectangle)
A Subprocess (blue rectangle) and an Assignment (green rectangle)
Two Collect information Steps (green rectangles)

practiceQuiz.hint: Every Process flow has exactly one green Start circle and one red End circle.
practiceQuiz.rationale: By default, every Process diagram includes a Start shape (green circle) and an End shape (red circle). The other shapes are added only when the configuration requires them.

practiceQuiz.scenario: A SA is reviewing a Pega Process diagram with a new team member who asks how to identify Decision shapes at a glance. In a Pega Process diagram, what color and shape represent a Decision?

options.text: An orange diamond
A yellow rectangle
A blue rectangle
A green rectangle

practiceQuiz.hint: Recall the shape and color used to represent a Decision node in a Pega Process diagram.
practiceQuiz.rationale: In the Pega Process diagram, shape color and geometry encode meaning: orange diamonds represent Decision shapes that branch the flow based on conditions. Yellow rectangles are Automation shapes that execute system logic. Blue rectangles are Subprocesses such as Approve/Reject. Green rectangles are Collect Information or Assignment shapes that require user interaction.

practiceQuiz.scenario: Create Case, Send email, and Change Stage appear in a Process diagram as which shape?

options.text: Yellow rectangles (Automation shapes)
Orange diamonds (Decision shapes)
Blue rectangles (Subprocesses)
Red circles (End shapes)

practiceQuiz.hint: Identify the color and shape category for automation steps like Send Email and Create Case.
practiceQuiz.rationale: Automation shapes such as Create Case, Send email, and Change Stage are yellow rectangles. Decisions are orange diamonds, Subprocesses are blue rectangles, and the End shape is a red circle.

practiceQuiz.scenario: An Approve/Reject Step appears in the Process diagram. What is its shape and color, and what category is it?

options.text: A blue rectangle — a Subprocess
An orange diamond — a Decision shape
A yellow rectangle — an Automation shape
A green circle — a Start shape

practiceQuiz.hint: Recall the shape color and category assigned to Approve/Reject Steps in the Process diagram.
practiceQuiz.rationale: In the Pega Process diagram, Subprocess shapes — including the Approve/Reject Step — are rendered as blue rectangles. This distinguishes them clearly from orange diamond Decisions, yellow rectangle Automations, and green Collect Information shapes. Knowing shape colors is essential for reading and troubleshooting any Process diagram in Pega.

practiceQuiz.scenario: What is the purpose of a Decision shape in a Process diagram?

options.text: To add a conditional path supporting more than one outcome, advancing the Process automatically based on business logic or one or more Conditions
To pause the Case until a user manually selects which path to follow
To send an outbound notification when a Step completes
To define what a user can do on the form at a specific Step

practiceQuiz.hint: A conditional path supporting more than one automatic outcome uses the Decision shape.
practiceQuiz.rationale: Decision shapes add a conditional path supporting more than one outcome and advance the Process automatically based on business logic or Conditions. B describes manual selection (the opposite). C is an Automation (Send notification). D describes a Flow Action.

practiceQuiz.scenario: A Decision flow needs to move the Case to a different Stage, skipping a Stage to support out-of-sequence processing. Which shape accomplishes this?

options.text: The Change Stage shape
The End shape
A Local Action on the Assignment
A Connector Action line shape

practiceQuiz.hint: Which specific shape in the Process diagram transitions a Case to a different Stage out of sequence?
practiceQuiz.rationale: One Decision flow variation uses the Change Stage shape to move the Case to a different Stage; skipping a Stage supports out-of-sequence processing. The End shape resolves the Case; Local and Connector Actions are Flow Actions, not Stage movers.

practiceQuiz.scenario: A Pega System Architect is configuring an Assignment Step and explains to a junior developer the purpose of a Flow Action in the context of user interaction during Case processing. What does a Flow Action define in a Pega Process?

options.text: What a user can do at a specific Step — controlling how users interact with forms while performing an Assignment
The full beginning-to-end path of a Process
The business logic that automatically branches the Case without user input
The Stage to which a Case is moved when it is created

practiceQuiz.hint: What a user can do at a Step.
practiceQuiz.rationale: Flow Actions define what a user does at an Assignment: which form shows, which fields appear, and which submit options are available. They control the user interaction, not the flow path.

practiceQuiz.scenario: A user clicks a button that completes the Assignment AND advances the Case to the next shape. Which Flow Action type is this, and how is it configured?

options.text: A Connector Action — configured as a line shape (the connector) in the Process Modeler
A Local Action — configured in the properties pane of the Assignment shape
A Decision shape — configured as an orange diamond
An Automation — configured as a yellow rectangle

practiceQuiz.hint: Which Flow Action type both completes the current Assignment and advances the Case to the next shape?
practiceQuiz.rationale: A Connector Action completes the Assignment and advances the Case to the next shape; it is configured as a line shape (the connector) in the Process Modeler. A Local Action does not advance the Case. Decision shapes and Automations are not Flow Actions.

practiceQuiz.scenario: A BA is evaluating whether to use Local Actions or optional Processes for single-step ad-hoc work in a Case workflow. Which TWO statements correctly describe a Local Action in Pega?

options.text: It updates the Assignment but does NOT advance the Case to the next shape
It is configured in the properties pane of an Assignment shape in the Process Modeler
It completes the Assignment and advances the Case to the next shape
It is configured as a line shape (the connector) between two shapes

practiceQuiz.hint: Local = updates in place; lives on the Assignment shape.
practiceQuiz.rationale: A Local Action updates the Assignment but does NOT advance the Case (A), and it is configured in the properties pane of an Assignment shape (B). C and D describe a Connector Action — it completes and advances the Case and is configured as a line shape.

practiceQuiz.scenario: A Pega System Architect is reviewing Process diagram shapes with a new developer. Which TWO statements correctly describe how shapes communicate their purpose in a Pega Process diagram?

options.text: Each shape type uses a specific color to indicate its purpose — for example, blue shapes represent utility Assignments
Connectors between shapes can carry Actions that execute as the flow transitions between steps
All Process diagram shapes are interchangeable and differ only in their visual label text
Decision shapes must always appear at the bottom of a Process diagram by design convention

practiceQuiz.hint: Shape color signals purpose in Pega Process diagrams, and Connectors can carry execution logic.
practiceQuiz.rationale: Pega Process diagram shapes are color-coded by type — for example, blue for Assignment steps, green for Subprocess steps, making the flow's intent visually clear. Connector Actions execute business logic (such as setting a property) during a flow transition. Shapes are not interchangeable and Decision shapes have no positional requirement.

practiceQuiz.scenario: A developer asks about the relationship between the Case Life Cycle and Process diagrams in Pega. Which TWO statements are correct?

options.text: Each Process in the Case Life Cycle corresponds to a Process diagram in the Process Modeler that defines the steps within it
Editing the Process diagram in the Process Modeler directly changes the Case processing logic at runtime
A Process diagram in the Process Modeler is documentation only and has no effect on what actually executes at runtime
Multiple Case Life Cycle Processes can share one Process diagram without any configuration

practiceQuiz.hint: The Process diagram IS the rule that executes — it is not just a visual document.
practiceQuiz.rationale: Each Process in the Case Life Cycle is backed by a Process (Flow) rule that is visualized as a Process diagram in the Process Modeler. Editing the diagram modifies the actual rule that executes at runtime — it is not merely documentation. Multiple independent Case Life Cycle Processes each require their own Process diagram.

quickRecap.value: A series of Steps expected to occur in a logical, sequential order.
Advanced shapes-and-connectors view (Process Modeler) for non-sequential paths to resolution.
Click the Configure Process icon on the Process → opens the Process Modeler.
Start = green circle; End = red circle; Collect/Assignment = green rect; Subprocess = blue rect; Automation = yellow rect; Decision = orange diamond.
Adds a conditional path supporting >1 outcome; advances automatically by business logic/Conditions; can include another Step or Change Stage (skip a Stage).
Defines what a user can do at a Step; associated with a connector or an Assignment shape.
Connector Action completes + advances (line shape); Local Action updates but does NOT advance (Assignment shape properties pane).
